57.title: Palms (Matthew 21:1–11)
57.hook: he rides in on a donkey and the crowd throws coats on the road
57.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday Catholics receive blessed palms, walk in procession, and hear the Passion read; many keep the palms at home until they are burned for the next Ash Wednesday, and every Mass sings hosanna in the Sanctus.

segments.voice: Last week ended at Lazarus's tomb, and the line Jesus wept. Now the road reaches Jerusalem. This is Holy Week.

Picture a parade. Presidents arrive in armored cars. Conquering generals in Rome rode in chariots, and kings entered cities on war horses. Everybody could see the power. Now it's springtime, just before Passover, and Jerusalem is packed with pilgrims. Jesus sends two disciples to a village on the Mount of Olives to fetch something for his entrance. Not a horse. A donkey, and her colt. They throw their cloaks over them, and he sits on them. The crowd goes wild. They spread their coats on the road and lay down branches cut from the trees. And they shout one word, over and over.
screen: `KINGS RIDE WAR HORSES.` → `HE SENDS FOR A DONKEY.` → `COATS AND BRANCHES ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The crowds cry out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, from a line in Psalm one hundred eighteen: hoshia na: save us, please. It began as a cry for help and became a shout of praise, like a cheer. Both meanings are in the air that day: help us, and hooray. The donkey is no accident. Matthew says it fulfills the prophet Zechariah: "Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass." A king, but a meek one, who comes in peace, not on a war horse. The whole city is stirred up, asking: who is this? And the crowds answer: this is Jesus the prophet, from Nazareth of Galilee. The Church relives this day every year on Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week. Palms are blessed, and people carry them in procession into the church. Then, in the same Mass, the whole Passion is read, and the mood turns: the crowd's hosanna and the cross, held together on one day. Many Catholics take their blessed palms home, tuck them behind a crucifix, and bring them back the next year, when old palms are burned to make the ashes for Ash Wednesday. And at every Mass, all year, Catholics sing this crowd's words in the Holy, Holy, Holy: hosanna in the highest.

segments.voice: Think about who arrives in your day: a child home from school, a coworker walking in late, a neighbor, a stranger at the door; most arrivals get a glance, or nothing. Choose one person and picture giving them a real welcome, eyes up, a smile, their name: not a parade, just a coat on the road. If you pray, you can say the crowd's word, hosanna, as praise or as a cry for help.
Hosanna. From Hebrew: save us, please. A cry for help that became a shout of praise, sung at every Mass. Today's word.
Your line: a king on a donkey. Power that comes in peace. Day fifty-seven, and Holy Week begins.

58.title: The tables overturned (Matthew 21:12–13)
58.hook: the one time he makes a whip, and it's about the house of prayer
58.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of the cleansing of the Temple on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year B, and many treat the season as a time to clear out habits and clutter to make room for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hosanna: the crowd's cry as a king rode in on a donkey. Your line was a king on a donkey. Today the gentle king shocks everyone.

The outer courts of the Temple in Jerusalem, a few days before Passover. Enormous, noisy, packed with pilgrims. They need animals for the sacrifices, so people are selling cattle and sheep and doves. They need the right coins for the Temple, so money changers sit at their tables. The shouting, the bargaining, the animals, the clink of coins. And Jesus walks in, the man who has spent weeks of our story healing, forgiving, eating with sinners, telling stories of lost sheep. And he starts turning over tables.
screen: `THE TEMPLE COURTS AT FESTIVAL.` → `SELLERS AND MONEY CHANGERS.` → `HE TURNS OVER THE TABLES.`

segments.voice: Matthew says Jesus cast out all who were buying and selling there, and overthrew the tables of the money changers, and the seats of those who sold doves. Coins rolling across the stone floor. Birds fluttering. People shouting. Then he quotes scripture, in the Douay-Rheims: "My house shall be called the house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves." He's joining two prophets: Isaiah, who promised that God's house would be a house of prayer, and Mark adds, for all nations; and Jeremiah, who warned against treating the Temple like a hideout for robbers. So this isn't Jesus against the Temple. It's a Jewish teacher who loves the Temple, standing in the line of Israel's own prophets, demanding that it be what it's for. The whip is in John's Gospel: he made a whip of cords and drove them all out, the sheep and the oxen too. A whip, in the hands of the man who told the story of the lost sheep, and he uses it to clear a space for prayer. And watch what happens next in Matthew. The blind and the lame come to him in the Temple, and he heals them. The space gets cleared, and then filled, with the people who needed it most. Catholics hear another layer too: Saint Paul writes that you yourselves are God's temple, and that his Spirit lives in you. The Church reads John's version of this story in Lent, a season for clearing out the clutter so there's room for prayer.

segments.voice: Think of a space in your life meant for one thing that has filled up with everything else: a desk, a corner of your room, the first ten minutes of your morning eaten by the phone, your own head. Picture the tables going over, gently, the clutter cleared and the space open again, and ask what you'd want that space to be for. If you pray, you can ask for a house of prayer inside you.

59.title: The perfume (Mark 14:3–9)
59.hook: a woman breaks a jar worth a year's wages over his head and he defends her
59.carry: she has done a beautiful thing
59.howItsDone: Catholics hear the anointing at Bethany in the Passion read on Palm Sunday in the year of Mark, and the Church's anointings with holy oils, at baptism, confirmation and ordination, echo the meaning of the word Christ, the anointed one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a whip of cords and the tables overturned. Your line was a house of prayer. Today, Bethany, two days before the Passover.

A dinner in Bethany, at the house of a man called Simon the leper. Jesus is reclining at the table with friends. Mark has just told us the chief priests and scribes are looking to seize him. The air is heavy. A woman walks in holding a small alabaster jar of precious spikenard, a costly perfume. It could have been sold, someone says, for more than three hundred denarii, and in Jesus's own parable of the vineyard, a denarius is a day's pay. She doesn't open it. She breaks it, and pours it out over his head. The smell fills the room. Nobody can pretend it didn't happen.
screen: `A DINNER IN BETHANY.` → `AN ALABASTER JAR OF NARD.` → `SHE BREAKS IT OVER HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Some of the guests are furious. Why this waste? It could have been sold, and the money given to the poor. They scold her. It sounds like a sensible point. But Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me." The Greek is kalon ergon, and kalon means both good and beautiful; that's why some modern translations say, she has done a beautiful thing. You'll always have the poor with you, he says, and you can help them whenever you want. It echoes the Law of Moses, which says the poor will not be wanting in the land, and so commands an open hand to them. But me, he says, you won't always have. She has done what she could. She's anointed my body ahead of time, for burial. She understood what was coming when the others didn't. Then a promise: "wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done, shall be told for a memorial of her." And here we are, telling it. Yet Mark never gives her name. John tells a similar story, also in Bethany, and says it was Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, and that she anointed his feet. In Mark, it's his head. And in the scriptures, a prophet anointed a king by pouring oil on his head, as Samuel did for Saul. Messiah means anointed one. She's the one who does it.

Think of one person who has given you more than you ever paid back, and picture breaking the jar for them: your whole evening, a long letter, real attention with the phone in another room. If you pray, you can offer God something lavish too: time, or thanks.
The perfume. A jar broken over his head, a room full of scent, and a woman remembered wherever the story is told. Today's word.
Your line: she has done a beautiful thing. And she's still remembered. Day fifty-nine, complete.

60.title: The basin and towel (John 13:1–15)
60.hook: at the last supper he kneels and washes their feet
60.carry: as I have done to you
60.howItsDone: At the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest washes the feet of members of the congregation, a rite called the Mandatum, after the Gospel of John 13 is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jar of perfume, and the line she has done a beautiful thing. Today, a towel.

Sandals, dusty roads, animals in the streets. When guests came in from the road, water was brought for their feet. In the scriptures, washing someone else's feet is a servant's work: when David sends for Abigail, she answers that she will wash the feet of his servants. The night before he dies, Jesus is at supper with his closest friends, and John says he knows his hour has come. John opens the scene, in the Douay-Rheims: "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end." To the very last. Then, in the middle of the meal, he gets up from the table.
screen: `DUSTY FEET, A SERVANT'S JOB.` → `THE LAST SUPPER.` → `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: John slows down and gives every movement. He rises from supper. He lays aside his outer garments and ties a towel around his waist. He pours water into a basin. He begins to wash the disciples' feet and dry them with the towel. The teacher is on his knees, doing the servant's job, friend by friend. Judas, who will betray him, is at that table, John has told us. His feet get washed too. Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it. Lord, are you going to wash my feet? Jesus says: you don't understand now, but you will. Peter: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus: "If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me." Then Peter swings the other way: then not only my feet, Lord, but my hands and my head. Afterward he dresses again, sits down, and asks: do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you're right. If I've washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's. "For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you do also." Catholics relive this on Holy Thursday, at the Mass of the Lord's Supper. Where the rite is kept, the priest sets aside his outer vestment, kneels, and washes the feet of people from the parish. The rite's old Latin name is the Mandatum, from Jesus's new commandment later that night, and it gives English the name Maundy Thursday.

61.title: Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36–46)
61.hook: he asks the cup to pass, then not my will but thine; they fall asleep
61.howItsDone: On Holy Thursday night Catholic parishes keep the Blessed Sacrament at an altar of repose so people can watch and pray with Jesus, and some Catholics keep a regular holy hour before the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandatum: at the last supper he knelt and washed their feet. Your line was as I have done to you. Tonight, a garden.

Supper is over. They sing a hymn and walk out of the city in the dark, down across a little valley and up into an olive grove on the far side. He tells most of them to sit and wait while he goes on to pray, and takes three with him: Peter, James and John. Then, Matthew says, he begins to grow sorrowful and to be sad, and he tells them so. In the Douay-Rheims: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death: stay you here, and watch with me." The one who calmed storms is asking his friends not to leave him alone. He goes a few steps further, falls on his face, and prays.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, IN THE DARK.` → `PETER, JAMES AND JOHN.` → `STAY YOU HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: The name Gethsemane most likely comes from Aramaic words for an oil press, a place where olives were crushed until the oil ran out. Matthew doesn't explain the name; he goes straight to the prayer: "My Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me. Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." The chalice, the cup, is an old biblical picture for what life pours out for you to drink; here it means the suffering coming at dawn. Notice he asks. He doesn't pretend he wants it. Luke even says his sweat fell like drops of blood. The Church teaches that Jesus had a real human will, and here you can hear it: a man who does not want to die, handing himself over anyway. Luke gives today's line, in the Douay-Rheims: "not my will, but thine be done." Then he walks back, and the three are asleep. "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" He isn't furious. He almost makes excuses for them: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak." Three times he prays. Three times they sleep. Catholics keep that hour. On Holy Thursday night, after the evening Mass, the Blessed Sacrament is carried to a side altar, and people come to watch with him into the night. Tradition ties the holy hour, an hour of prayer before the Eucharist, to that same question.

The job is only to stay: hold them in mind, and when you notice you've drifted to your own list, come back, the way he came back to his sleeping friends. If you pray, you can simply pray for them.

62.title: Peter's three denials (Luke 22:54–62)
62.hook: a servant girl asks, a cock crows, and the Lord turns and looks at Peter
62.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Peter's denial in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and many bring their own failures to God in the sacrament of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gethsemane, the oil press: let this chalice pass, and his friends asleep. Your line was not my will. Now, a courtyard.

It's the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house. Peter, the one who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, has followed at a distance, all the way into the courtyard. Somebody has lit a fire. It's cold. Peter sits down with the others around it, trying to look like everyone else. A servant girl looks at him in the firelight. Looks again. And says, to the whole circle, this man was with him too. Peter answers before he thinks. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, I know him not." That's the first one.
screen: `A FIRE IN THE COURTYARD.` → `A SERVANT GIRL LOOKS TWICE.` → `WOMAN, I KNOW HIM NOT.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it in three quick blows. The girl. A little later, another person: you're one of them. Peter: I am not. About an hour on, a third insists: this man was with him, for he's a Galilean too. And Peter says he doesn't even know what the man is talking about. While he's still speaking, a rooster crows. Then the verse only Luke has: "And the Lord turning looked on Peter." Jesus is somewhere in that courtyard, under guard, close enough to turn. Peter remembers what Jesus told him at supper: before the cock crowed, he would deny him three times. "And Peter going out, wept bitterly." Here's the honest part: Luke never tells us what that look was like. Christians have read it for centuries as mercy, not anger, because of what comes after. Peter isn't written off. On Easter morning, Luke says, he's the one who runs to the tomb. And this is the same Peter Jesus called the rock. The first pope, in Catholic teaching, is a man who failed his friend three times in one night and was not given up on. The Church was built on someone who knew exactly how much he needed mercy. That's why Catholics say a failure is never the last word, and why they say confession exists: you go out, you weep, and you come back.

Don't argue with it; let it be true, then picture a look coming toward you across the courtyard, not anger, something that knows and stays. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in your own plain words.

63.title: Before Pilate (John 18:28–19:16)
63.hook: Pilate asks what is truth and washes his hands
63.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of the trial before Pilate every Good Friday, and they name Pilate each Sunday when they profess the Creed at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's three denials, the rooster, and the Lord turning to look. Your line was the look was not anger. This morning, a governor.

Early morning. Jesus is led to the headquarters of the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. In John, the council tells Pilate they have no power to put anyone to death. That power is Rome's. What follows is almost a stage play. Pilate walks outside to the crowd, back inside to his prisoner, out again, in again. Outside, voices getting louder. Inside, a quiet man in chains, and a governor who can't work out who he is. And here's a strange thing: at Sunday Mass, in the Creed, Catholics say this man's name, a few words after the name of Mary. The old Apostles' Creed puts it: suffered under Pontius Pilate.
screen: `THE ROMAN GOVERNOR'S HOUSE.` → `OUT TO THE CROWD, BACK TO THE PRISONER.` → `SUFFERED UNDER PONTIUS PILATE.`

segments.voice: Pilate starts with the question that matters to Rome: are you a king? A king is a rival. Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world." Pilate presses. Jesus says he was born and came into the world to give testimony to the truth, and that everyone who is of the truth hears his voice. Then Pilate says the line: "What is truth?" And he doesn't wait. John says he goes straight back out. A sneer? Tired? An honest question? The text doesn't tell us his tone. Later readers found a wordplay in it: in Latin the question is quid est veritas, and shuffle those letters and you get est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here. Nobody in the story says that. But it's the Christian answer: the truth was standing in front of him. Three times Pilate says he finds no fault in him. And still he hands him over to be crucified. Matthew adds a picture: Pilate takes water and washes his hands in front of the crowd, as if that settled it. It didn't. The hands were washed; the choice was still his. It was Rome that carried out the execution. And the Catholic Church teaches plainly, at the Second Vatican Council and in its Catechism, that his death cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, or against the Jews of today.
